opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting direction, and I think it's one of the more promising ways to get value out of the enormous amount of driving data we collect but never label.

The basic intuition is this. If a model can look at the past few seconds of camera, lidar, and radar and accurately predict what the next few seconds of sensor data will look like, it has to have internalized a lot about the world. It needs to understand the 3D geometry of the scene, how the ego vehicle's motion changes the viewpoint, which things are static and which are moving, and roughly how other agents behave: that a car in the left lane is probably going to keep going, that a pedestrian at the curb might step out. None of that has to be labeled explicitly. The future frames are the supervision signal, and you get them for free.

That matters because in autonomous driving the expensive part has always been labeling. Drawing 3D boxes, tracking objects, annotating semantics, all of that costs a lot and doesn't scale to the long tail. Meanwhile a fleet generates millions of miles of raw sensor logs. Future prediction lets you turn that raw data into a training objective, which is very much what made language models work. Next-token prediction on huge corpora gave you a strong foundation, and then you fine-tune for specific tasks.

There are some important nuances, though. First, what level do you predict at? Predicting raw pixels is very high-dimensional, and the model can waste a lot of capacity on things that don't matter for driving, like the exact texture of leaves or lighting changes. So there's a lot of interest in predicting in a more abstract space: future occupancy, future lidar point clouds, which are geometric and fairly clean, or future latent features, in the spirit of JEPA-style approaches. Lidar forecasting is attractive because it directly tells you about free space and geometry, which is what you care about for safety.

Second, the future is multimodal. Given the same past, many futures are plausible, and a naive regression loss will blur them together. You need a generative formulation, whether diffusion, autoregressive tokens, or something similar, that can represent several possible outcomes. That ties nicely into behavior prediction and planning, where reasoning over multiple futures is exactly what you need.

Third, conditioning on the ego vehicle's actions is powerful. If you predict future sensor data given what the car plans to do, you're basically learning a world model. That gives you a pretraining objective and potentially a simulator too: you can roll out counterfactuals, ask "what if I'd braked earlier," and use that for evaluation or closed-loop training.

As for how it helps downstream: the representations from that pretraining tend to transfer well to perception tasks like detection and segmentation, and to motion forecasting and planning, often with much less labeled data to reach the same quality. It also seems to help on the rarer cases, because the model has seen far more raw situations than you could ever label.

I'd add a caution: pretraining is not the whole story. You still need targeted supervision, careful evaluation, and safety validation, especially for the rare, high-consequence events. But as a way to build a foundation that really understands scene dynamics, predicting future sensor data is a very natural and scalable objective, and I expect it to be a big part of how driving models get built.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I'm pretty excited about, and I think it's actually one of the more natural analogues we have to what happened with large language models. If you think about what next-token prediction does for a language model, it forces the model to build an internal representation of how the world described in text works, because that's what it takes to predict what comes next. Driving has a version of that too. The vehicle is constantly receiving a stream of sensor data, camera images, lidar returns, radar, and the question "what will this stream look like half a second from now, or two seconds from now?" is an enormously rich prediction problem.

To predict the next lidar sweep or the next camera frame well, the model has to implicitly understand a lot of things. It has to understand geometry, where the static world is and how it moves relative to the ego vehicle as you drive forward. It has to understand that the car in front of you is an object that moves coherently, that it's going to keep going at roughly its current velocity unless something happens, that the pedestrian at the crosswalk might step out. It has to understand occlusion, that things disappear behind a truck and reappear on the other side. So the supervisory signal is essentially free, we have petabytes of logged driving data, and it's dense, you get a target for every pixel or every point rather than a single label per frame.

Contrast that with how we traditionally trained perception models, which is with human-labeled 3D boxes, segmentation masks, and so on. Labeling is expensive, it's slow, and the label vocabulary is fixed by whoever designed the taxonomy. So you end up with models that are good at the things you labeled and know very little about everything else, the long tail, the weird configurations you never anticipated. A model pretrained to predict future sensor data has to represent all of that whether you labeled it or not, because it all affects what the sensors will see next.

Now I'd be careful about a few things. One is that naively predicting raw pixels tends to waste capacity on things that don't matter for driving, like the exact texture of leaves on a tree or the specific noise pattern in a lidar return. So a lot of the interesting work is in choosing the right prediction space, whether that's a learned latent representation, or predicting at the level of occupancy and flow in 3D, rather than raw sensor values. The other is that the ultimate goal isn't perception for its own sake, it's driving well. So the question we always ask is whether the representations you learn this way transfer to the downstream tasks, prediction of other agents, planning, and so forth, and whether they do so with less labeled data and better robustness in the tail. The early evidence I've seen is encouraging, but the real proof is in those downstream metrics.

So in short, I see it as a way to get a kind of world model for free from the data we already collect, one that's more general than anything we could get from labels alone, and then specialize it for the actual driving task.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very promising direction because we collect a lot of driving data, and most of it is unlabeled. If you train a model to predict what the sensors will observe next, the future observations themselves provide a training signal.

To do that well, the model has to learn something about the structure of the world and how it evolves: which objects are moving, how they interact, and how the motion of our own vehicle changes what we see. The hope is that those representations give you a much better starting point for learning perception, prediction, and ultimately driving behavior.

The challenge is that the future isn’t deterministic. A car approaching an intersection might turn or go straight. You want a model that can represent those possibilities, rather than average them into something that isn’t physically meaningful. And you want it to focus on the aspects of the scene that matter for driving, rather than spend all its capacity predicting every detail of appearance. So the pretraining objective is important, but the real test is whether it improves the downstream driving system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very promising direction because we have so much driving data that isn’t labeled. If you ask a model to predict what the sensors will observe next, it has to learn something about the structure of the scene and how it evolves: which things are moving, how they interact, and how the vehicle’s own motion changes what it sees.

That could give you a useful representation before you train on more specific tasks like perception, prediction, or planning. You’re learning from the raw experience rather than requiring a human annotation for every example.

The challenge is that the future isn’t deterministic. There are multiple things another road user could do, and you don’t necessarily want to spend all your capacity predicting every pixel. So the question is how to formulate that prediction task so that the model learns the aspects of the world that actually matter for driving.
